Measures to improve tax collection\nSeveral measures have been implemented by the Federal Government throughout 2019 and 2020 to\nincrease tax revenues:\n Elimination of universal compensation. Until 2018, VAT positive balances could be\nrecovered by offsetting other taxes automatically and without prior authorisation from tax\nauthorities. This opened space for tax evasion by using fake invoices to reduce tax liabilities. In\n2019, universal compensation was eliminated, which increased tax revenues by 0.5% of GDP\nin 2020.\n Strengthening sanctions. As of 2020, crimes related to tax fraud are classified as serious\ncriminal offences and the issuance of fake invoices are considered organized crime activities.\nThis aims at deterring tax evasion by increasing the perception of the risk of being detected and\nby hardening sanctions if found guilty.\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 28, "locator": "page 28", "text": "26 \n Implementation of BEPS. In 2020, 5 of the 15 Actions of the BEPS project were implemented.\nThese measures could increase revenues by up to 0.4 percentage points of GDP by 2024.\n Taxing digital services. As of 2020, complexities for paying VAT for goods and services\nprovided by international platforms offering intermediation services or digital goods were\nremoved. The allocation of responsibilities across different levels of government in Mexico\nMexico is a federal country with a three-tier government structure. It is divided into 32 sovereign states.\nEach state is composed of municipalities, about 2 454 of them in the whole country. The federal\ngovernment is responsible for matters relevant for the whole country, such as macroeconomic policy,\ndefence and research and development policy (OECD, 2013[1]). The states are responsible for the\ndelivery of education and health. States are also co-responsible, together with the federal government\nand municipalities, for poverty alleviation and water management. Municipalities are purely responsible\nfor local matters such as water distribution and are co-responsible for school building and\nimplementation of social programmes with the federal and state government. The three levels of\ngovernment are involved in infrastructure and transportation. Federal and state governments execute\nroads construction, while states or municipalities mainly do maintenance (OECD, 2013 ). Federal\n[11]\ntransfers finance the bulk of sub-national expenditure, in particular in the areas of health and education.\nTransfers from the federal government amount to 92% of total subnational resources, the largest share\namong OECD countries with decentralised government structures. Sub-national governments’ own-\nsource revenues, for both states and municipalities, account for a small share of total tax revenues,\napproximately 6.7%, representing 0.9% of GDP. States and municipalities have full autonomy to set\ntheir own tax rates and/or bases over the payroll tax, vehicle taxes, property taxes, and user fees.\nStrengthening the fiscal framework\nMexican authorities have been for some time considering ways to further strengthen Mexico’s fiscal policy\nframework, as a way to safeguard and benefit fully from the credibility that Mexico has been gaining over\nthe years. Buttressing the fiscal framework would also help enhance Mexico’s ability to forestall future\ncrises, rebuild fiscal buffers, and respond to shocks. The short-term priority for fiscal policy is to continue\nto support the ongoing recovery. Advancing with initiatives to upgrade the fiscal framework, even if\nimplemented in the medium-term, would also have a favourable short-term impact, as they would boost\nconfidence.\nMexico has three fiscal rules in place (Box 1.4). However, the rules do not provide a truly countercyclical\npolicy framework and tend to favour pro-cyclical fiscal stances. The two budget balance rules favour that\nfiscal targets are met through discretionary spending cuts and they lack a link with a medium-term fiscal\nanchor. Mexico could introduce a debt limit, replacing the two balanced budget rules, to anchor fiscal policy\nover the medium-term, complemented with an enhanced spending rule. The coverage of the existing\nspending rule, at 36% of public sector expenditure, is too narrow, hampering its ability to smooth spending\nover the cycle. Enhancing the spending rule by widening the share of public spending covered, leaving out\nonly interest payments, would limit fiscal policy pro-cyclicality more forcefully.\nBox 1.4. Mexico’s fiscal rules\nThe current fiscal framework includes three fiscal rules:\n Balanced budget rule. The federal budget can only run a deficit of up to 2 % of GDP if it is due\nto public investment by the federal government and some States Owned Enterprises (such as\nPemex).\n Public sector borrowing requirement (PBSR) rule. Legislation requires that a target for the PBSR\nis specified in the budget document. This target is defined as achieving a non-increasing net\npublic debt path relative to the previous year. This rule affects all public sector entities except\nsubnational governments and the central bank.\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 38, "locator": "page 38", "text": "36 \n Structural current spending rule. The real growth rate of structural current spending is capped\nto potential output growth. Structural current spending is defined as programmable spending\nexcluding interest payments, cost of fuels for electricity generation, physical and financial\ninvestment of the federal government, pensions, and the expenditures of Pemex and the\nelectricity public utility company. As a result the rule covers 36% of public sector expenditure.\nThe upgrade of the rule could be complemented with a review and modernisation of the stabilization funds.\nThere are currently two stabilization funds, one for the federal and one for sub-national entities. Both funds\nreceive a share of the annual oil revenues, and aim at compensating for reductions in revenues with\nrespect to those approved in the budget in a given year. Thus, the funds in their current configuration do\nnot truly act as countercyclical tools, but mostly as revenue stabilizers. Creating a truly countercyclical\nfund, allowing saving in good times and spending during downturns, would increase Mexico’s ability to\nsmooth out cycles and protect more the economy against possible contingencies. Simplifying the rules to\naccess the funds and focusing the funds on stabilizing revenues over the cycle, and not with respect to\nbudgeted revenues, are good options to move in that direction.\nThe impact of an enhanced fiscal rule would be strengthened by introducing a multi-year expenditure\nframework. These frameworks have proven to be an effective tool to optimise public expenditure over the\nmedium-term and ensure support to government strategic priorities. Today, almost all OECD members\nhave a multiyear framework and they are being increasingly used among emerging economies. Mexico\ncould also establish a fully-fledged multi-year expenditure framework, building on its recently improved\nbudget preparation.\nMexico’s budgetary process has significantly improved overtime, gaining transparency and accountability.\nThe budget is analysed and debated with the legislative branch for over two months. This process could\nbe supported and further enhanced by establishing an independent an adequately resourced fiscal council,\nas recommended in the previous OECD Economic Survey (OECD, 2019 ). By providing non-partisan\n[10]\nfiscal analysis, fiscal councils can enrich the fiscal policy debate and help to communicate fiscal risks and\npolicy options. Fiscal Councils in emerging economies: the Chilean case\nChile has been gradually strengthening its fiscal framework over the last decades, which has\ncontributed to sustain economic growth and keep public debt relatively low. A fiscal rule helped to shield\npublic spending from the copper boom, generating savings that proved crucial when the country face\nnegative shocks, such as the global financial crisis. Assessing the monetary policy transmission in Mexico\nThe interest rate pass-through is a measure of the effectiveness of monetary policy. In particular, it\nassesses which percentage of a change in the short-term monetary policy reference rate is passed onto\nbank lending rates faced by households and firms. How fast market lending rates react to changes in\nthe monetary policy reference rate is another indicator of the effectiveness of the monetary policy. A\nfaster reaction points to a more effective monetary policy. Estimates of pass-through and speed of\nadjustment for four Mexican lending rates (Table 1.7 and (Maravalle, forthcoming )) indicates that\n[19]\nthere is significant heterogeneity in monetary policy transmission. The pass-through is significant for\nthe reference lending rate. Mortgage lending rates and automotive loan lending rates, instead, are less\nsensitive to changes in the monetary reference rate. In most cases, it takes within two to three months\nto fully adjust. However, for the mortgage lending rate it takes longer, around one year.\nTable 1.7. The estimation is based on a\nAutoregressive Distributed Lag model with Error Correction Term à la (Pesaran, Shin and Smith, 2001[20]).\nSource: OECD calculations based on (Maravalle, forthcoming[19]).\nThese estimates suggest that transmission is stronger in those segments of the financial market\nfocused on lending to firms than in markets lending to households. As an\nincreasingly open economy, Mexico’s exposure to global economic shocks has increased notably.\nEstablishing an unemployment insurance scheme would be key both from macroeconomic and social\nprotection angles. However, these early withdrawals hinder\nfuture pensions and provides less protection to workers that are more vulnerable. Providing income support to informal workers during the pandemic recession\nReaching informal workers is a challenge for public policies. Out of tax or social benefit systems and,\nin many cases, without access to banking services, many informal stay out of the radar of public policies.\nSeveral countries in Latin America successfully launched innovative schemes to reach them and\nprovide them with income support during the pandemic recession. An overview of the constitutional reform of the electricity market\nA constitutional reform proposal of the electricity market was announced in September 2021. The\nproposal will be discussed with key stakeholders and investors and is expected to be debated in\nCongress in 2022. With that reform, the Ministry of Energy aims at ensuring energy security, maintaining\nconventional plants as backups for renewables and at avoiding the oversupply of renewables permits,\nwhich exceeds the capacity of the grid and creates geographical unbalances. The proposal aims at\nphasing out some elements in private contracts which are deemed to be detrimental to the finances of\nthe state-owned Federal Electricity Commission (Comisión Federal de Electricidad or CFE) and of the\ngovernment, such as the subsidizing of the transmission fees. The proposal also aims at tackling\nproblems in the design of self-supply mechanisms, such as the creation of a parallel electricity market.\nThe initiative also attempts to redesign mechanisms to issue permits, particularly for renewables, to\nmitigate the oversupply problem. The reform proposal establishes a guaranteed market share of at least\n54% for CFE. The constitutional reform also expands CFE’s role in the oversight of the sector and\neliminates independent sector regulators. CFE would also be in charge of setting tariffs and granting\npermits. The electricity reform also changes the rules for generators to access the grid, prioritizing the\ndispatch of electricity generated by the state-owned company. Prior to the reform, access to the grid\nwas based on marginal power generation costs, giving priority to the least expensive generated\nelectricity, which is renewables-based and largely generated by the private sector. Conversely,\nelectricity generated by the state company is coming from hydroelectric, geothermal and nuclear\ncentrals or is fuel-based.\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 67, "locator": "page 67", "text": " 65\nTable 1.12. Access\nis also significantly unequal across income levels, gender, between rural and\nurban areas and across regions. SMEs access to bank credit is low,\nhampering firms’ ability to grow and innovate. The use of cash and informal\ncredit is still widespread, especially in rural areas, where financial\ninfrastructure is underdeveloped. The diffusion of digital financial services is\nslowly advancing but remains low, hindered by a relatively low level of\nfinancial literacy and a digital divide. Expanding access to finance would\nenable Mexican households to invest in education and health, and better\nmanage income shocks and smooth consumption. It would also enable\nMexican firms to invest more, increase productivity and create formal jobs.\nLow-income households, small firms and more disadvantaged regions would\nparticularly benefit, as it would unlock new economic opportunities for them.\nBoosting competition in the banking sector would facilitate SMEs access to\ncredit by lowering interest rate margins. Upgrading the regulatory framework\nof the financial system would help increase competition and quality of\nfinancial services. The potential of the fintech sector is yet to be materialised,\nwhich would further increase competition and bring financial services to wider\nsegments of the population. Strengthening financial education and digital\nliteracy would facilitate a larger and better use of traditional and digital\nfinancial services.\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 78, "locator": "page 78", "text": "76 \nMexico has large room for improving financial depth and increasing access to finance. Despite recent\nimprovements, it suffers from structural issues that have historically delayed its financial development,\nincluding low levels of financial literacy, a large informal sector, a costly enforcement of collateral\nrepossession and mistrust in the banking sector. Access to financial services is significantly unequal across\nincome levels, gender, between rural and urban areas and across states. Around one-eighth of Mexico’s\nmunicipalities does not have even one financial access point, though most of them are located in rural\nareas not densely inhabited. Even if 92% of the adult population has access to a bank branch, in some\nstates this share is significantly lower and reaches 56% in Oaxaca, 62% in Tlaxcala and 77% in Puebla.\nRegional disparities are reduced but remain when considering the access to any financial point. While\naround 98% of the population has access to one financial point, the share is as low as 81% in Oaxaca,\n93% in Chiapas and 94% in Yucatan. The gender gap remains significant in the access to some financial\nservices such as retirement savings.\nImproving access to financial services and deepening financial markets can help boost growth, promote\nemployment creation and reduce inequalities (OECD, 2017 ; OECD, 2019 ). Increasing depth (e.g. the\n[1] [2]\nsize of bank credit to the private sector and of the stock and the bond markets) and access to financial\nproducts is positively correlated to economic growth (OECD/The World Bank, 2012 ; Sahay et al., 2015 ;\n[3] [4]\nDabla-Norris et al., 2015 ). Financial inclusion can be especially beneficial for emerging economies\n[5]\nbecause an increase in its level appears to be linearly and positively related to growth (Sahay et al.,\n2015 ). It is also associated to sharp declines in income inequality and poverty rates in countries at\n[4]\nintermediate and advanced stages of financial development, provided that the pace of credit expansion\ndoes not lead to financial instability (Rajan, 2005 ) because of poor regulation and supervision (Mehrotra\n[6]\nand Yetman, 2015 ).\n[7]\nAs the access to financial services extends to a larger part of the population, and is no longer limited to\nthe wealthy, it tends to benefit more lower-income households (Greenwood and Jovanovic, 1990 ; Clarke,\n[8]\nXu and Zou, 2006 ; Jahan and McDonald, 2011 ), allowing them to invest in education, health and\n[9] [10]\nbusiness opportunities, and manage income shocks as to smooth consumption, thus helping them to avoid\npoverty. With the vast majority of poor households working in the large informal sector, extending financial\ninclusion is a component of the comprehensive strategy required to reduce informality in Mexico, as further\ndiscussed in chapter 1 of this survey.\nExpanding access to finance also offers significant synergies with other policy objectives. It can support\nthe transition to a lower carbon economy by providing the private sector with better financing opportunities\nto invest in green technologies that can help to respond to climate change mitigation and adaptation\nchallenges. Boosting financial inclusion can also support social protection policies by providing access to\nfinancial products that are attuned to the possibilities and needs of the more vulnerable population. Better\naccess to finance can also help to reduce gender inequalities in wage and labour participation rate, which\nare large in Mexico (see chapter 1). Wider access to digital financial services can foster women\nentrepreneurship, particularly in digital activities.\nThis chapter describes the main barriers to the development of financial markets in Mexico and discusses\navailable policy options to tackle them. It also discusses complementary factors for financial development,\nsuch as reforms to improve competition among financial institutions as well as other economic reforms.\nFor example, extending internet coverage would support mobile banking and help reduce regional\ninequalities. Expanding financial inclusion also requires a balance between public policy and private sector\ninitiative. The government’s role is also to provide a supportive regulatory environment that fosters\ncompetition and growth, as well as strong independent supervisory institutions that maintain financial risks\nin check. It is crucial to balance financial deepening with financial stability and consumer protection\ncontrols. The private sector on the other hand, can harness technological innovation and develop new\nproducts and business models to support financial inclusion.\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 79, "locator": "page 79", "text": " 77\nFirms’ and individuals’ access to finance is low\nMexico ranks low in key financial inclusion indicators compared to both advanced economies and regional\npeers (Figure 2.1). For example, the share of adults with a bank account is low and so is the number of\nbank branches per 100 thousand adults. Only around 47% of the population aged between 18 and 79years\nof age held a bank account in Mexico in 2018, less than in other OECD members in the region such as\nCosta Rica (68%) and Chile (74%).\nIndicators of financial depth, such as bank loans to households and bank deposits as a share of GDP,\nprovide a similar picture (Figure 2.2). Credit guarantee programs facilitate credit access to SMEs in\n[18]\nMexico. Around 45% of all commercial bank credit to SMEs in 2020 was covered by credit guarantees\nprovided by the development bank Nacional Financiera and, for export oriented firms, by the Banco\nNacional de Comercio Exterior Credit. However, SMEs’ access to bank credit is lower than in the average\nOECD country and regional peers such as Colombia and Chile (Figure 2.5). Improving access to financial\nservices would intensify firm creation and growth, benefitting particularly small firms and start-ups (Guiso,\nSapienza and Zingales, 2004 ). Deeper and more inclusive financial markets, by easing financing\n[19]\nconstraints, tend to help especially SMEs grow more (Rajan and Zingales, 1998 ). In underdeveloped\n[20]\nfinancial systems, increasing the access of SMEs to finance also contributes to reduce inequality (Banerjee\nand Duflo, 2005 ), as unequal access to credit is a barrier to economic opportunities and entrepreneurial\n[21]\nactivity. Financial development, by helping poor entrepreneurs without collateral to access credit supports\ntheir formalisation.\nA high interest rate margin (Figure 2.6, Panel A), well above what is observed in Chile or other OECD\ncountries, is one of the principal barriers to credit for SMEs. The spread between SMEs and large firms’\nloan rates is also relatively high (Figure 2.6, Panel B). Financing constraints are a main barrier to growth\nof SMEs in underdeveloped financial systems (Beck and Maksimovic, 2005 ), and hinder formalisation\n[22]\nas entrepreneurs who fail to raise funding tend to operate in the informal sector (Banerjee and Duflo,\n2005 ). Access to bank credit can also be particularly challenging for young and innovative firms that do\n[21]\nnot have collateral or a credit track record. In\nMexico there are three companies in charge of collecting credit history information for firms and individuals\n(credit bureau), two of them belonging to the same economic group. Since then, the share of adults using a debit or a credit card has increased, but their use\nremains limited: the number of credit card transaction per adult is very low in international comparison and\nonly 55% of credit card holders used it in 2019 (CNBV, 2020 ).\n[66]\nThe use of cash remains dominant in Mexico. Most adults who are financially included use cash for small\n(90%) and large (78%) payments (ENIF, 2018 ). Preference for cash and, to a lesser extent, mistrust in\n[33]\nthe financial sector are the main reasons for not using a debit card (ENIF, 2018 ). Older adults and\n[33]\nindividuals living in rural areas are also far less likely to use digital payments, which points to an important\ndigital and financial education gap across generations and between rural and urban areas (ENIF, 2018 ).\n[33]\nRegional gaps are also relevant, with Ciudad de Mexico, Quintana Roo and in general Northern states\nlargely outperforming the other states in number of digital transactions (Figure 2.13. , Panel A). This creates a good momentum for the digitalisation of payments that could be reinforced\nby additional policy efforts.\nThe diffusion of digital payments is a priority to effectively promote financial inclusion and inclusive growth\nas digital payments favour the access to other financial services (Demirguc-Kunt, Klapper and Singer,\n2017 ). Digital payments also lower the cost, and increase the speed, of making and receiving payments.\n[17]\nThis is especially relevant in rural areas where distances to a government office, bank branch or money\ntransfer operator may be large, which further highlights the need for extending digital infrastructure to rural\nunderserved areas. They reduce security risks associated to handling cash, helping to reduce the\nincidence of crime (Wright et al., 2014 ) and allow for direct payment of government transfers, thus\n[67]\nincreasing transparency and reducing the risk of bribes (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar, 2014 ).\n[68]\nThey may contribute to reduce the gender gap by granting women control over the transfers received in\ntheir account, thus reducing the possibility of a kinship tax (Morawczynski and Pickens, 2009 ).\n[69]\nDigital payments may also help build a credit record, thus facilitating households’ access to credit and\nallowing financial institutions a better credit risk assessment (Cook and McKay, 2015 ). This is especially\n[70]\nrelevant in large informal economies like Mexico where the use of cash is more widespread (GPFI,\n2018 ). Digitalisation has the potential to grant firms and individuals that operate in the informal sector a\n[71]\ngreater chance to access formal financial products, thus boosting financial inclusion. Current regulation prevents the entry of competitors to the unique domestic digital payment\n[74]\nsystem (Box 2.5) because of uncertainty about what rules, operational standards and costs would apply to\ndigital payments involving a buyer (cardholder) and a seller (business) using different payment systems\n(cross-system transaction). In the absence of a clear regulation on cross-system transactions, the potential\nrisk is that the network administrator of the dominant domestic payment system would impose its rules and\ncosts as to prevent price competition. This risk deters the entry of new players (COFECE, 2020 ) in the\n[74]\npayment card market where the overall degree of concentration remains high, with the five largest banks\naccounting for about 80% of the market (Bátiz-Zuk and Lara Sánchez, 2021 ).\n[23]\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 111, "locator": "page 111", "text": " 109\nThe authorisation process of a new clearing house participating in the digital payment system should be\namended to guarantee impartiality. Currently, such authorisation is conditional on the technical approval\nof incumbent clearing houses, which are required to ensure interoperability among different payment\nsystems. This technical approval, however, should be subject to a time limit, which is currently absent, thus\nprovoking an excessively lengthy authorisation procedure. Also, the liquidity guarantee of digital payment\ntransactions should be shifted from the company to the clearing house, who holds better information to\nevaluate the counterpart risk, to incentivise competition.\nVertical integration between banks participating to the digital payment system (issuers or acquirers) and\nthe clearing house should be discouraged. The payment card market in Mexico\nThe payment cards market is a two-sided market where a payment card company acts as a platform by\nselling card services to cardholders (buyers) and, through a point-of-sale terminal (POS), to businesses\n(sellers). The card payment system can be closed or open. In the closed system the credit card company\ndirectly provides POS services to sellers and issues cards to buyers, without intermediaries. In the open\nsystem, instead, a payment card company provides card and POS services to buyers and sellers\nindirectly through banks or other financial intermediaries (Figure 2.28). Accordingly, cardholders buy\ncard services from a bank (issuer) and businesses buy POS services from another bank (acquirer). In\nan open card payment system, when a cardholder buys a product from a seller, the transaction is cleared\nat the level of the two banks by a clearing house, which is responsible of the authentication, authorisation,\ncompensation and liquidation of any card payment.\nFigure 2.28. However, so far Visa Mexico and MasterCard Mexico have not yet become operational.\nRealising FinTech’s potential\nFintech has the potential to accelerate the development of digital payments, boost financial inclusion and\nincrease competition in the financial system. Such potential remains so far unrealised. Mexico was a\npioneer with the Fintech law in 2018, however, its full effects have not yet materialised since a slow\nauthorisation process of new fintech firms was experienced in part related to a natural learning curve\nexperienced during the initial phase of implementation of the law. However, the aforementioned challenges\nare expected to dissipate over time. Technical disruptions that limit the\navailability of digital payments are frequent and the number of digital frauds is increasing, with online\nfinancial frauds representing 70% of all financial frauds in the first quarter of 2021. This has negative\nrepercussions on the level of trust in digital payments and their diffusion. Temporary regulatory sandboxes\nfor fintechs, allowed by the Fintech Law, have the potential to promote financial innovations (OECD,\n2020 ) by enabling fintechs to experiment with new financial products and services temporarily and in a\n[75]\ncontrolled environment. The access could become permanent conditional on the absence of security\nissues following a congruent observational period. Fintech-bank partnerships\nFintech-bank partnership may increase financial inclusion by providing low-income consumers\naffordable financial services (credit and savings, person-to-person transactions, business-to-person\ntransactions) through technologies including biometric identification, on-boarding, cloud computing and\nopen application programming interfaces (APIs) (to facilitate integration of IT systems within and\nbetween institutions, and across sectors, thus promoting competition and transparency) and distributed\nledger technology to make verification and completing transactions faster and easier. These\npartnerships are also mutually beneficial. Banks benefit from the possibility of offering new products,\nreaching a larger customer base and improving product efficiency and customer experience. Fintechs\nget access to capital and scale their technology.\nOne of the fintech areas with great potential for financial inclusion is the deployment of artificial\nintelligence (AI) models in lending, to reduce the cost of credit underwriting and facilitate the extension\nof credit to ‘thin file’ clients, potentially promoting financial inclusion (OECD, 2021). The use of AI can\ncreate efficiencies in data processing for the assessment of creditworthiness of prospective borrowers,\nenhance the underwriting decision-making process and improve the lending portfolio management. It\ncan also allow for the provision of credit ratings to ‘unscored’ clients with limited credit history,\nsupporting the financing of the real economy (SMEs) and potentially promoting financial inclusion of\nunderbanked populations (OECD, 2021). The strategy of the Central Bank to promote financial inclusion\nThe Central Bank of Mexico aims to promote transparency, efficiency and competition in the provision\nof financial services, while ensuring consumers protection. In carrying out its function of oversight over\nthe financial system it strikes a balance between harnessing the opportunities provided by technological\ninnovation to expand financial inclusion and limiting the risks for the stability of the financial system and\nthe consumers represented by the introduction into financial markets of new products and new players.\nMore generally, the strategy followed by the Central Bank in exerting its oversight over the area of digital\nfinancial services is summarised by the following principles:\n1) Adopting the principle of “same activity, same risk same regulation”.\n2) Enforcing interoperability and net neutrality in the offer of digital financial services.\n3) Fostering competition and avoiding mergers among dominant players.\n4) Ensuring operational continuity with large providers.\n5) Achieving international coordination to address jurisdictional gaps.\n6) Ensuring full customer protection.\n7) Strengthening the standards for cybersecurity.\nBoosting digital skills to facilitate diffusion of digital financial services\nIn Mexico there are still too few students with the skills to thrive in the digital era, as shown by an average\nPISA score in reading, math and science that is below the average OECD country (see chapter 1). Early\ndisadvantage in acquiring foundation skills leads to further disadvantages when it comes to the acquisition\nof further skills and competencies later in life and policies should aim at a widespread diffusion of basic\nliteracy and numeracy skills (OECD, 2020 ). The acquisition of a good level of cognitive skills and a\n[80]\nhigher educational attainment appear to enable a more diverse and complex internet use (OECD, 2020 ),\n[61]\nincluding of digital financial tools.\nExcessive cost of training and lack of time because of child care responsibilities are the two main barriers\nto access training for informal workers and non-workers, having prevented around half of them from\nengaging in training despite willing to do so (Box 2.8). Strengthening the child care network, as discussed\nin Chapter 1, would facilitate women’s uptake of training opportunities and help them to improve their digital\nskills. Vouchers, grants, stipends and scholarship targeting digital skill training can help to reduce or\neliminate the direct and opportunity costs of skills training for informal workers. Drawing on OECD country\nexperience in basic skills programmes, free digital skill programmes could be provided via specialised\ncentres (as in Flanders in Belgium and Ontario in Canada) or through a system of vouchers which\nindividuals may use in training centres of their choice (as in Vienna in Austria) (OECD, 2017 ; OECD/ILO,\n[81]\n2019 ; Palmer, 2020 ).\n[82] [83]\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 116, "locator": "page 116", "text": "114 \nBox 2.8. (2014), “Less Cash, Less Crime: Evidence from the Electronic Benefit Transfer [67]\nProgram”, NBER Working Papers No. 19996, http://dx.doi.org/10.3386/w19996.\nOECD ECONOMIC SURVEYS: MEXICO 2022 © OECD 2022"}, {"unit": 127, "locator": "page 127", "text": "OECD Economic Surveys\nMEXICO\nMexico is recovering from a pandemic that had deep economic and social impacts. Informal workers, women\nand youth were particularly hit, exacerbating long‑standing social challenges. Mexico’s solid macroeconomic\npolicy framework safeguarded macroeconomic stability. But medium term growth prospects have weakened\nand growth over the past two decades has been low. Poverty rates and regional inequalities remain high.\nInformality, financial exclusion or corruption have hindered productivity growth. Low female participation\nrates and weak investment since 2015 have also impacted medium‑term growth prospects. Maintaining\nand strengthening Mexico’s solid macroeconomic policy framework is key for stability. The ability of fiscal policy\nto smooth out economic cycles and support growth during recessions can be enhanced, creating more space\nfor public investment. Rebooting private investment and turning around low productivity growth are fundamental\npriorities. This will require comprehensive reforms to improve business regulations, boost competition,\nreduce informality and corruption and transition towards carbon neutrality. Prensa / México Evalúa identifica una tendencia al autoritarismo presupuestal\nMéxico Evalúa / 26 de mayo de 2022\nMéxico Evalúa identifica una tendencia al autoritarismo presupuestal\nEn su análisis de los principales indicadores de finanzas públicas al primer trimestre del año, México Evalúa observa que el presupuesto ejercido es muy diferente al aprobado por el Congreso en septiembre del año pasado, producto de las decisiones discrecionales de un Ejecutivo sin contrapesos reales."}, {"unit": 2, "locator": "extracted HTML block 2", "text": "Para mantener los balances presupuestales y al mismo tiempo liberar recursos para un gasto que cumple con los intereses políticos del Gobierno, se han cortado importantes programas sociales y de obra pública.\nAl tiempo que demuestra que el gasto público no es el que necesita el país, México Evalúa reafirma su llamado a lograr una mejor gobernanza del erario, mediante mecanismos institucionales de contrapeso y rendición de cuentas.\nCiudad de México, a 25 de mayo de 2022\nA través de los Números de Erario , su plataforma de análisis de finanzas públicas con un enfoque ciudadano, México Evalúa ha identificado que el erario garantiza cada vez menos financiamiento a los programas y servicios públicos de primera necesidad –como el de la salud para personas sin seguridad social–, y cada vez más al servicio del grupo en el poder.\nComo resultado de un crecimiento insuficiente de los ingresos públicos y una toma de decisión discrecional por parte del Gobierno federal (sin rendición de cuentas ni mecanismos de vigilancia), se han ejecutado recortes sustantivos en diversas áreas del erario: 40% de los programas presupuestarios con presupuesto aprobado . Al parecer se hizo con el fin de adelantar el gasto de los programas de transferencias directas ‘consentidos’ del Ejecutivo, como las Pensiones de Adultos Mayores, el programa de transferencias con el mayor presupuesto (el cual, cabe señalar, es regresivo, porque beneficia más a quienes más tienen).\nEn efecto, los indicadores de finanzas públicas al primer trimestre del año sugieren un uso político-electoral del erario , muy alejado de los estándares del sistema democrático y, en última instancia, de las más apremiantes necesidades de la sociedad mexicana, México Evalúa observa."}, {"unit": 3, "locator": "extracted HTML block 3", "text": "Más allá de que el presupuesto ejercido sea distinto al aprobado por el Congreso a fines del año pasado, sin que se hayan explicado las conveniencias de esto, y de la evidente falla de gobernanza que esto implica, los Números de Erario encontraron indicios preocupantes tanto en el renglón de ingreso como en el de gasto del Sector Público .\nImpulso insuficiente de los ingresos, que enciende focos rojos\nEl análisis muestra que los ingresos totales del Sector Público se han colocado en mejores niveles que en 2019, a pesar de que la economía mexicana no ha recuperado su nivel prepandemia. Los ingresos petroleros han revivido a causa del aumento de precios del crudo; no obstante, la renuncia del Gobierno a cobrar el IEPS de combustibles (que tienen el objetivo de evitar que los precios al consumidor se disparen) han limitado esta ganancia. El mayor impulso a los ingresos proviene de un crecimiento en la recaudación vía Impuesto Sobre la Renta, y esto se ha dado principalmente por una mayor fiscalización de los grandes contribuyentes, no por mayor dinamismo en la economía.\nAdemás, no se verificó la hipótesis de que los ingresos petroleros con sus excedentes iban a alcanzar para cubrir la renuncia del Gobierno federal de cobrar el IEPS . Frente al calendario se debían recaudar 350 mil millones de pesos (mmdp) en el primer trimestre por estos dos conceptos; no obstante, se lleva un retraso o una pérdida de 40 mmdp por la política de subsidios a los combustibles que directamente beneficia más a quienes más tiene."}, {"unit": 4, "locator": "extracted HTML block 4", "text": "Conclusión: hay un claro riesgo en el financiamiento público por populismo fiscal , pues el Gobierno mantiene importantes renuncias a cobrar impuestos, la tributación pende de un hilo (de la recaudación secundaria: fiscalización de asalariados y grandes contribuyentes), mientras que la recaudación primaria, la cual es impulsada por la economía, se encuentra debilitada: el IVA muestra una caída de 9.3% (29.9 mmdp).\nGasto público excedido en los rubros con agenda política y abandono de la salud e inversión\nEl gasto público total está estancado como consecuencia del bajo crecimiento de los ingresos. Aumentó un poco en relación con el año pasado, menos de 1%, pero a diferencia del ingreso, no cumplió con la meta de gasto aprobada para el primer trimestre. Esto significa que en el agregado se observó un subejercicio. Pero al desagregar el gasto México Evalúa identificó aumentos que se concentraron en pocos programas presupuestarios , directamente relacionados con la agenda del Ejecutivo: transferencias a Pemex, algunos programas sociales (Pensión para adultos mayores y Becas para el Bienestar), el Tren Maya y en menor medida el Corredor Interoceánico.\nParalelamente, se confirmó que la salud no es prioridad en el presupuesto. En el agregado ha caído el presupuesto para financiar los subsidios a la atención de la salud para las personas sin seguridad social, ya sea por el Insabi o IMSS-Bienestar. La transición del Insabi al IMSS-Bienestar no tiene el financiamiento necesario como para convertirse en una realidad tangible, lo que anuncia un nuevo fracaso y, por ende, un impacto en el bolsillo de los mexicanos que utilizaban estos servicios, y en el posible deterioro de su salud de quienes no puedan cubrirlos con esquemas alternos."}, {"unit": 5, "locator": "extracted HTML block 5", "text": "Ante este panorama, México Evalúa recomienda:\nEl Gobierno debe diversificar su recaudación para que su crecimiento no dependa de una sola apuesta, que es la fiscalización de los grandes contribuyentes. Esto requiere, entre otros factores, dejar de impulsar una agenda política sin sentido económico o en contra de la inversión privada y, por el contrario, dar certidumbre jurídica y operar políticas públicas a favor del crecimiento económico.\nNo renunciar a cobrar el IEPS . Es recomendable financiar, con los recursos de su cobro, un programa de subsidios a los precios de los alimentos y posiblemente de otros bienes para los hogares económicamente más vulnerables.\nFocalizar adecuadamente los programas sociales , que además deben mejorar su progresividad (que resulten más beneficiados los que menos tienen).\nImpulsar desde la sociedad civil y la oposición mecanismos de contrapeso y rendición de cuentas para que las autoridades puedan hacer adecuaciones al presupuesto durante su ejercicio (ya sea para cambiar su financiamiento o para cambiar las asignaciones presupuestarias, sobre todo entre instituciones), pero sin comprometer el financiamiento a los programas y proyectos que garantizan derechos.\nDespolitizar la agenda de inversión pública : es imperante desarrollar proyectos de infraestructura para el desarrollo económico y la provisión de servicios públicos, así como actualizar y dar mantenimiento a los existentes.\nPUEDEN CONOCER LOS HALLAZGOS COMPLETOS DE LOS NÚMEROS DE ERARIO, AQUÍ\nPUEDEN ACCEDER A LOS INDICADORES QUE SOSTIENEN EL ANÁLISIS DE LOS NÚMEROS DE ERARIO, AQUÍ"}, {"unit": 6, "locator": "extracted HTML block 6", "text": "Contacto de prensa\nCynthia Castañeda\n55 2302 9582\n[email protected]\nContenido relacionado\nGastos catastróficos en salud se disparan 64.5% en 2024 frente a 2018: México Evalúa\njulio 31, 2025\nCumbre de Latinoamérica y el Caribe: es tan importante elevar la tributación como lograr un gasto público progresivo\njulio 28, 2023\nPosibilidades para una reforma al impuesto sobre la renta de las personas\nseptiembre 9, 2021\nMéxico Evalúa es un centro de pensamiento y análisis que se enfoca en la evaluación y el monitoreo de la operación gubernamental para elevar la calidad de los resultados. Learn more × Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search\nStatistics > Applications\narXiv:2108.02653 (stat) [Submitted on 4 Aug 2021 ( v1 ), last revised 16 Mar 2022 (this version, v3)]\nTitle: Practices of public procurement and the risk of corrupt behavior before and after the government transition in México\nAuthors: Andrea Falcón-Cortés , Andrés Aldana , Hernán Larralde View a PDF of the paper titled Practices of public procurement and the risk of corrupt behavior before and after the government transition in M\\'exico, by Andrea Falc\\'on-Cort\\'es and 1 other authors View PDF\nAbstract: Corruption has a significant impact on economic growth, democracy, and inequality. It has severe consequences at the human level are incalculable. Public procurement, where public resources are used to purchase goods or services from the private sector, are particularly susceptible to corrupt practices. However, government turnover may bring significant changes in the way public contracting is done, and thus, in the levels and types of corruption involved in public procurement. In this respect, México lived a historical government transition in 2018, with the new government promising a crackdown on corruption. In this work, we analyze data from more than 1.5 million contracts corresponding from 2013 to 2020, to study to what extent this change of government affected the characteristics of public contracting, and we try to determine whether these changes affect how corruption takes place. To do this, we propose a statistical framework to compare the characteristics of the contracting practices within each administration, separating the contracts in different classes depending on whether or not they were made with companies that have now been identified as being involved in corrupt practices. We find that while the amount of resources spent with companies that turned out to be corrupt has decreased substantially, many of the patterns followed to contract these companies were maintained, and some of those in which changes did occur, are suggestive of a larger risk of corruption."}, {"unit": 2, "locator": "extracted HTML block 2", "text": "Comments: 20 pages of main text and 15 of supplementary material.
